# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm)

This comment is valuable. Its attrition finding and its record-based and timesheet corrections are exactly the checks the Halden working paper needed, and its Data note honestly limits the estimates to the subsets studied. But its conclusion goes much further than its own analysis supports, and it misreads the Varden trial, which is the strongest evidence it cites.

The arithmetic checks out, with one exception:
- 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%.
- 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, so 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%.
- 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, so 95.4 / 86.1 = +10.8%.
- 1.014 / 1.041 = −2.6% real revenue.
- The hours decomposition doesn't add up (see section 2 below).

## 1. The main conclusion contradicts the evidence the authors rely on

**"Entirely an artifact" doesn't follow from the analysis.**
- After the corrections, a 10.8% per-hour gain remains. The abstract calls this "plausibly a novelty effect," but by the conclusion it has become "entirely an artifact."
- The authors never test the novelty explanation (see section 4). A plausible alternative explanation is not the same as showing there is no real effect.

**The Varden trial points the other way.** The authors call Varden "the most reliable finding in the literature" but cite only its counter-office result.
- Varden also found per-hour gains of +12.5% in case-processing (CI +6.9 to +18.4) and +6.7% in counter offices.
- Those gains used randomisation, record-based output and timesheet hours.
- That design rules out selection, manager reporting and scheduled-hours denominators, the main artifacts this comment identifies.
- Novelty remains possible, but Varden ran for nine months against a randomised control.
- The authors can't treat Varden as most reliable for the negative result while leaving out its positive one.

**The claim is too general.**
- A re-analysis of one pilot, in subsets the Data note itself calls non-random, can't support a conclusion about "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- The defensible conclusion is narrower: the Halden pilot's 23.4% is mostly measurement and selection, and the leftover gain of about 11% is of uncertain durability.

## 2. Problems within the corrections

**The abstract misdescribes Table 2.**
- The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. The first three are attrition, the output measure and the hours denominator.
- Table 2 corrects only output and hours; attrition is never quantified.
- The paper needs either a bounding exercise or an intent-to-treat analysis. That would mean including the nine withdrawals with pessimistic assumed outcomes, for example no gain or output at their last observed value.
- Until then, "attrition accounts for part of the gain" is a plausible direction, not an estimate.

**The rows of Table 2 use different samples.**
- The rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations.
- Each step down the table therefore mixes the effect of the correction with changes in which organisations are included.
- All four specifications should be shown within the 17-organisation subset, so each correction's contribution can be separated out.

**The hours decomposition is inconsistent.**
- The authors explain the hours gap as longer days (+0.7 hours on each of four days, 2.8 hours) plus 1.6 hours on the day off. That totals 4.4 hours.
- Added to 32 scheduled hours, this gives 36.4 hours a week, not the reported 34.6.
- The paper should reconcile these figures.

**Record-based output isn't automatically the true value.**
- In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher than the records, a consistent gap worth taking seriously.
- But the records are partial measures (tickets closed, units produced), and "billable hours delivered" is itself an hours measure.
- Part of the 3.8-point gap could be things managers count and the records miss.
- The authors should report results separately by type of record.

**The revenue correction is sensible but approximate.** CPI is a rough deflator for sector output prices. The sign of the conclusion probably survives, but the authors should say the deflator is approximate.

## 3. The attrition finding is the strongest contribution

The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show seven of nine withdrew after the schedule began, and six cited workload. If that holds, the working paper misdescribed its own data on a point that matters.

The comment should say so clearly and ask the Halden authors for an explanation. As written, it lets this finding drop out, and the conclusion states it as settled fact ("removed the organisations least able to cope") without ever having estimated its size.

## 4. The novelty argument is untested even though the data exist

- **The extrapolation is wrong.** A straight line through 0.61 at month 3 and 0.29 at month 6 falls by about 0.107 a month. It reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." Extrapolating a straight line from two points is itself fragile.
- **Energy isn't output.** A fall in self-reported energy doesn't show that productivity fell.
- **The direct test is available.** The pilot's output index was collected *monthly*, and time-tracking logs cover the whole period. The authors could test whether output per actual hour declined from month 1 to month 6 in the 17-organisation subset. That would bear directly on the novelty claim, and the comment doesn't do it.
- **The burden-of-proof argument has limits.** It is a fair reason to be cautious about durability. It isn't evidence that the gain is zero.

## 5. Section 7 misrepresents the Varden trial

- **Varden didn't present the meetings analysis as a mechanism.** It said explicitly that the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, and "cannot establish a mechanism." It also registered a confirmatory test. Varga & Holm's warning that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" responds to a claim Varden didn't make.
- **The seven offices weren't a post hoc subgroup.** They were the entire treated case-processing stratum, which was defined before randomisation.
- **The data weren't collected after the results were known.** Calendar data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results. What was post hoc was the correlational analysis, not the choice of offices or the timing of the data.
- **The underlying caution is fair.** A correlation across seven offices is weak evidence, and Varden says so. The section should be rewritten to engage with what Varden actually wrote.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Retail.** The "fall of 11.2%" in retail and hospitality rests on three organisations. It should be presented as illustrative, with that sample size stated.
- **The Varden comparison.** Varden's counter offices are public-sector contact centres, not retail. Their output fall is relevant but isn't direct evidence about retail.
- **Hedging versus overclaiming.** "In our assessment" appears twice next to "entirely." The hedge doesn't fit the strength of the claim.

## Bottom line

The comment's core empirical points are credible and important:
- non-random attrition, apparently misreported in the working paper;
- systematic upward bias in the manager-reported index;
- a 14% rather than 20% cut in actual hours;
- a real fall in revenue;
- the per-hour metric being mechanically guaranteed to show gains.

Together these bring Halden's 23.4% down to about 11% in the subset that can be checked.

Its conclusion should be revised to match. A defensible version would read: "The Halden pilot overstates the per-hour gain by more than half. The residual is of uncertain durability. Randomised evidence (Varden) suggests real but smaller per-hour gains where output is not tied to presence, and losses in output per employee where it is." The paper should also quantify attrition, put each correction on a common sample, run the monthly novelty test, and correct its account of Varden's meetings analysis.
